Outliers and dataset tests

Source: vignettes/outliers.Rmd
outliers.Rmd

Six tests compare records within a species or dataset rather than against external reference data. These include outlier, which identifies geographic outliers within a species; three fossil outlier tests; and dataset_ddmm and dataset_rounded, which detect coordinate conversion and gridding errors across a dataset. They correspond to CoordinateCleaner’s cc_outl(), cf_age(), cf_outl(), cf_range(), cd_ddmm(), and cd_round().

Unlike record-level tests, these tests need all records in a group before they can evaluate any of them. They therefore run in a separate pass over the input, before the record-level tests.

This article demonstrates the geographic and dataset tests using simulated alpine plant records. It also introduces the artificial-hotspot test aohi and explains how the group pass handles streamed input. The fossil tests are covered in Cleaning fossil records, and installation instructions are available in Get started.

Example data

The table contains 961 records of four alpine plant species from the Eastern Alps, distributed across three datasets. Salix retusa is represented by only six records. Four herbarium records far outside their species’ ranges (New York, Sydney, Paris and Moscow) are added, plus one Pinus mugo record within its range as a control. A column truth labels each record.

Two datasets of 300 records each are also added, to test for systematic coordinate errors. In the first, coordinates were incorrectly converted from degrees and minutes to decimal degrees, leaving no fractional part above .59. In the second, coordinates fall on the centres of a quarter-degree grid.

Simulation code 
library(OccurrenceCleaner)

set.seed(11)
sp <- data.frame(species = c("Erica carnea", "Gentiana verna", "Pinus mugo", "Salix retusa"),
                 lon = c(12, 10, 14, 11), lat = c(47, 46.5, 47.5, 46.8), sd = c(1.5, 2, 1, 1.2),
                 n = c(400, 250, 300, 6))
x <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(sp)), function(i)
  data.frame(species = sp$species[i], decimalLongitude = round(rnorm(sp$n[i], sp$lon[i], sp$sd[i]), 5),
             decimalLatitude = round(rnorm(sp$n[i], sp$lat[i], sp$sd[i] / 2), 5))))
x$datasetKey <- sample(c("survey-a", "survey-b", "herbarium"), nrow(x), TRUE)
x$truth <- "clean"
far <- data.frame(species = c("Erica carnea", "Erica carnea", "Gentiana verna", "Pinus mugo", "Pinus mugo"),
                  decimalLongitude = c(-74.0, 151.2, 2.35, 12.1, 37.6), decimalLatitude = c(40.7, -33.9, 48.86, 47.3, 55.8),
                  datasetKey = "herbarium", truth = c("far", "far", "far", "clean", "far"))
ddmm <- data.frame(species = sample(sp$species[1:3], 300, TRUE),
                   decimalLongitude = floor(runif(300, 8, 16)) + sample(0:59, 300, TRUE) / 100,
                   decimalLatitude = floor(runif(300, 45, 48)) + sample(0:59, 300, TRUE) / 100,
                   datasetKey = "atlas-ddmm", truth = "ddmm")
grid <- data.frame(species = sample(sp$species[1:3], 300, TRUE),
                   decimalLongitude = round(runif(300, 8, 16) * 4) / 4 + 0.125,
                   decimalLatitude = round(runif(300, 45, 48) * 4) / 4 + 0.125,
                   datasetKey = "atlas-grid", truth = "grid")
x <- rbind(x, far, ddmm, grid)
head(x, 3)
#>        species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude datasetKey truth
#> 1 Erica carnea         11.11345        48.00728   survey-b clean
#> 2 Erica carnea         12.03989        46.22010   survey-a clean
#> 3 Erica carnea          9.72517        47.88716   survey-a clean
table(x$datasetKey, x$truth)
#>             
#>              clean ddmm far grid
#>   atlas-ddmm     0  300   0    0
#>   atlas-grid     0    0   0  300
#>   herbarium    302    0   4    0
#>   survey-a     326    0   0    0
#>   survey-b     329    0   0    0

Geographic outliers 

f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier"))
table(truth = f$truth, outlier = f$flag_outlier)
#>        outlier
#> truth   FALSE TRUE
#>   clean   957    0
#>   ddmm    300    0
#>   far       1    3
#>   grid    300    0

Three of the four distant records are flagged, while no clean records are flagged. For each species, the test calculates every record’s mean distance to all other records of that species. The threshold is the 75th percentile of these mean distances (Q75) plus five times their interquartile range (IQR, the spread between the 25th and 75th percentiles); a record whose mean distance exceeds it is flagged, following CoordinateCleaner’s default.

The Gentiana verna record in Paris is not flagged. The simulated Gentiana records span about 2 degrees of longitude around 10° E, so the Paris record, at 2.4° E, does not increase the mean distance enough to exceed the threshold. Salix retusa is not tested because its six distinct locations fall below the default min_occs = 7.

The threshold and distance statistic can be changed through settings. With method = "mad", the threshold is the median of the mean distances plus five times their median absolute deviation (MAD, the median of the distances from that median). With method = "distance", a record is flagged if its nearest other record of the same species is more than tdi kilometres away (1000 km by default):

m <- sapply(c("quantile", "mad", "distance"), function(meth)
  tapply(flag_occurrences(x, tests = "outlier", settings = list(outlier = list(method = meth)))$flag_outlier,
         x$truth, sum))
knitr::kable(m)
quantile mad distance
clean 0 3 0
ddmm 0 9 0
far 3 4 3
grid 0 3 0

The MAD threshold is the stricter one here: it catches all four far records but also 15 records inside the species’ areas, most of them in the converted atlas, whose coordinates are shifted towards the south-west of each degree square. The distance method flags the same three far records as the quantile threshold; the Paris record is within 1000 km of Gentiana records in the Alps. The map shows the default result:

plot(f, type = "map", rules = list(outlier = "outlier"))

CoordinateCleaner’s sampling correction leaves outliers unflagged in countries with few records, where an isolated record is more likely a real but poorly documented population than an error. It works in three steps:

  1. A table of record counts per country is passed as gazetteers = list(sampling = ...).

  2. Each country’s record density is compared with the densities of all countries in the table. The quantile sampling_thresh of these densities is the threshold.

  3. An outlier keeps its flag only when its country’s density lies above the threshold; in the other countries the flag is lifted.

counts <- data.frame(country = c("US", "AU", "FR", "RU", "AT", "DE", "IT", "CH", "SI"),
                     records = c(4e8, 1.2e8, 1e8, 6e6, 2.5e7, 1.8e8, 5e7, 4e7, 6e6))
fs <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier"), gazetteers = list(sampling = counts),
                       settings = list(outlier = list(sampling_thresh = 0.25)))
x[fs$flag_outlier != f$flag_outlier, c("species", "decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude")]
#>          species decimalLongitude decimalLatitude
#> 957 Erica carnea            -74.0            40.7
#> 958 Erica carnea            151.2           -33.9
#> 961   Pinus mugo             37.6            55.8

Russia, Australia and the United States have the three lowest densities in this table, at or below its 25 % quantile, so the outlier flags on the records in Moscow, Sydney and New York are lifted. The counts here are illustrative. Real ones come from rgbif::occ_count(country = ...) for each country, or from a tally of the input itself. The table is recorded in the reference label by size and checksum.

Species with many records

For a species with 10,000 records or more the pairwise distances are replaced by a raster approximation, as in CoordinateCleaner: records are counted on a 0.5-degree grid spanning the whole input, the statistic is computed between grid cells with distances weighted by the cell counts, and the records of the outlier cells are flagged. settings = list(outlier = list(thinning = TRUE)) uses the grid for every species, and thinning_res sets the cell size. A species of 15,001 records with one record in Madrid:

big <- data.frame(species = "Rhododendron ferrugineum",
                  decimalLongitude = c(rnorm(15000, 11, 1.5), -3.7),
                  decimalLatitude = c(rnorm(15000, 46.8, 0.6), 40.4))
system.time(fb <- flag_occurrences(big, tests = "outlier"))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    0.02    0.00    0.03
which(fb$flag_outlier)
#> [1] 15001

The Madrid record is the only one flagged. CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1 flags no records on this path; Compatibility with CoordinateCleaner shows the comparison.

Dataset tests 

d <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded"))
knitr::kable(aggregate(as.data.frame(d)[c("flag_dataset_ddmm", "flag_dataset_rounded")],
                       by = list(dataset = d$datasetKey), FUN = all))
dataset flag_dataset_ddmm flag_dataset_rounded
atlas-ddmm TRUE FALSE
atlas-grid FALSE TRUE
herbarium FALSE FALSE
survey-a FALSE FALSE
survey-b FALSE FALSE

dataset_ddmm flags every record of the converted atlas and dataset_rounded every record of the gridded one; the three datasets of clean records pass both. The dataset key is datasetKey, GBIF’s identifier of the publishing dataset, and can be set with occ_columns(dataset = ...). Records without a key are not tested. The two tests read different signs, which the decimal parts of the coordinates show:

library(ggplot2)
dec <- data.frame(dataset = x$datasetKey,
                  lon = x$decimalLongitude %% 1, lat = x$decimalLatitude %% 1)
dec <- dec[dec$dataset %in% c("survey-a", "atlas-ddmm", "atlas-grid"), ]
ggplot(dec, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "#2E6F9E") +
  facet_wrap(~dataset) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "decimal part of longitude", y = "decimal part of latitude") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))

The two tests look for different patterns in a dataset’s coordinates.

dataset_ddmm detects incorrect conversions from degrees and minutes to decimal degrees. In correctly converted coordinates, the decimal part can range from 0 to 1. With the conversion error, it never exceeds 0.59. The test looks for this missing range using a binomial test on a 1000 × 1000 grid.

dataset_rounded detects coordinates placed on a regular grid. Instead of taking many different values, the coordinates occur at fixed intervals. The test identifies this spacing through the autocorrelation of latitude and longitude histograms.

In this example, the degree-minute atlas has the conversion error but no regular grid. The gridded atlas has decimal parts of 0.125, 0.375, 0.625 and 0.875 on both axes, but no conversion error. Each atlas is therefore flagged by only one test.

Artificial hotspots 

ah <- reference_points("aohi")
h <- data.frame(species = "Erica carnea", decimalLongitude = ah$lon[ah$taxon == "Plantae"][1:3] + 0.03,
                decimalLatitude = ah$lat[ah$taxon == "Plantae"][1:3])
data.frame(hotspot = ah$notes[ah$taxon == "Plantae"][1:3],
           flagged = flag_occurrences(h, tests = "aohi")$flag_aohi)
#>                       hotspot flagged
#> 1            zero coordinates    TRUE
#> 2  Reserva Natural La Planada    TRUE
#> 3 center of a 4km grid square    TRUE

aohi flags records within 10 km of a point of the Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023): the coordinates that recur most often in GBIF plant, bird, insect and mammal records, such as (0, 0), a nature reserve or the centre of a mapping-grid square. The inventory’s notes and determination columns say why a point recurs and whether it is a real observation site, so it can be filtered before use (Custom reference points and polygons).

One rule over all of them 

all_f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded", "aohi"))
t <- tally_flags(all_f, by = "datasetKey",
                 rules = list(grouped = c("outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded", "aohi")))
knitr::kable(t[, c("datasetKey", "n", "flagged_outlier", "flagged_dataset_ddmm",
                   "flagged_dataset_rounded", "flagged_aohi", "removed_grouped", "kept_grouped")])
datasetKey n flagged_outlier flagged_dataset_ddmm flagged_dataset_rounded flagged_aohi removed_grouped kept_grouped
atlas-ddmm 300 0 300 0 1 300 0
atlas-grid 300 0 0 300 3 300 0
herbarium 306 3 0 0 4 6 300
survey-a 326 0 0 0 0 0 326
survey-b 329 0 0 0 0 0 329

Both atlases are removed entirely. The herbarium loses six records: three geographic outliers and four records near known artificial hotspots, with one record flagged by both tests.

The New York record lies 5 km from Central Park, a bird-recording hotspot. The Paris record, which passed the outlier test, lies 3.7 km from the centre of a French 10 km mapping grid cell. Two otherwise clean records in Bavaria are also flagged because they lie near centres of the German floristic mapping grid.

The aohi flags in the atlases reflect similar patterns. Whether these records should be removed depends on whether grid-centre coordinates are suitable for the analysis.

Streamed input

For input stored across multiple files, the group pass runs before the record-level tests. It reads all files twice. The first pass counts records per species and determines the coordinate range of each dataset. The second collects the information needed to test each group.

To limit memory use, small species groups and fossil taxa are written to hashed bucket files, large species are counted on a grid, and dataset summaries are updated as records are read. This avoids loading the entire input into memory.

Records of the same species or dataset are tested together, even when spread across files. The results are saved in group_result.rds in the output directory, so a resumed run can skip the group pass. Splitting the example table into three files produces the same tally as processing it as a data frame:

src <- file.path(tempdir(), "parts"); dir.create(src, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (i in 1:3) vectra::write_vtr(x[seq(i, nrow(x), 3), ], file.path(src, sprintf("part-%d.vtr", i)))
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "flags-grouped")
s <- flag_occurrences(src, tests = c("invalid", "outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded"),
                      out = out, keep = c("species", "datasetKey"), verbose = FALSE)
st <- tally_flags(s, by = "datasetKey", rules = list(grouped = c("outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded")))
identical(st$removed_grouped, tally_flags(flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "outlier", "dataset_ddmm",
                                                                       "dataset_rounded")),
                                          by = "datasetKey",
                                          rules = list(grouped = c("outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded")))$removed_grouped)
#> [1] TRUE

The flags agree record by record as well; the package’s tests check that for every grouped test, including the fossil tests with their random age draws.

Practical guidance

  • A grouped flag depends on the rest of the input. Adding records of a species can turn an outlier into a normal record, and removing a dataset’s records changes nothing for the other datasets. Run the grouped tests on the table that goes into the analysis, after taxonomic filtering, not on a larger extract.

  • The quantile threshold is the conservative default. At Q75 + 5 x IQR it flagged three of four far records and no clean one here; the MAD threshold flagged all four plus 15 records inside the species’ areas. mltpl moves either threshold.

  • Species below min_occs distinct points are not tested. With fewer than 7 points the spread of the distances says little; min_occs can be raised, not usefully lowered below a handful.

  • The dataset tests need a dataset key and a reasonable span. dataset_ddmm tests only datasets spanning at least min_span degrees (2) on both axes; dataset_rounded needs at least min_unique_ds_size distinct points (4) and reads histogram regularities, so a small or highly clustered dataset can be flagged by it without being gridded. Its result is best read per dataset, with tally_flags(by = "datasetKey"), before it goes into a rule.

  • A raster approximation answers a coarser question. For species of 10,000 records or more, a cell of 0.5 degrees is the unit: a single far record forms its own cell and is flagged, but an outlier cell next to the main range is not.

References

Park DS, Xie Y, Thammavong HT, Tulaiha R, Feng X (2023). Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (AHOI). Journal of Biogeography 50:441-449. doi:10.1111/jbi.14543

Zizka A, Silvestro D, Andermann T, Azevedo J, Duarte Ritter C, Edler D, Farooq H, Herdean A, Ariza M, Scharn R, Svanteson S, Wengström N, Zizka V, Antonelli A (2019). CoordinateCleaner: standardized cleaning of occurrence records from biological collection databases. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10:744-751. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13152
